title: Steak and Kidney Pie
subtitle: Chuck steak and ox kidney in a rich gravy, under a shortcrust lid
excerpt: The classic British pie: chunks of beef and ox kidney slow-braised in a dark, thick gravy of ale and stock, then topped with a golden shortcrust pastry lid and baked. A dish for cold-weather comfort.

recipe.sourceNotes: Steak and kidney pie is one of the defining dishes of British working-class cooking, with the combination of beef and kidney appearing in recipe collections from the mid-nineteenth century. Mrs Beeton included a version in her Book of Household Management (1861), and the dish became a standard of pub and canteen cooking through the twentieth century. The combination of ox kidney with beef chuck provides a layering of flavour: the kidney adds iron and richness, the beef provides body and structure. The pie is distinct from a steak and kidney pudding (steamed in suet pastry) and from a steak and kidney pot pie (with a pastry top only rather than a full encased pastry shell). Traditional versions use Guinness or dark ale as part of the braising liquid.

recipeTools.notes: A deep pie dish of around 1.5 litres capacity.
A large, heavy casserole for the initial braise.
A frying pan for browning the meat in batches.

content.text: Brown the meat in batches in a very hot pan: crowding causes steaming rather than browning and a grey, flavourless filling results. Soak the ox kidney in cold water for 30 minutes before using; this mellows the strong metallic edge. The filling must be completely cooled before topping with pastry or the steam will make the base soggy.

items.preparation: soaked in cold water for 30 minutes, trimmed of sinew and cut into 2 cm pieces
seasoned with salt and pepper, for dusting

content.text: Toss the beef and kidney in the seasoned flour to coat lightly. Heat the oil in a large casserole over high heat. Brown the meat in batches until deeply coloured on all sides; remove each batch and set aside. Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and mushrooms and cook for 2 minutes.

Return the meat to the pan. Add the wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes. Add the stock, Worcestershire sauce, thyme, and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, cover tightly, and cook over the lowest possible heat for 1.5 to 2 hours until the beef is very tender. The sauce should be thick and glossy. Remove the thyme sprigs and bay leaves. Cool completely.

Heat the oven to 200 C (180 C fan). Spoon the cold filling into a deep 1.5-litre pie dish. Roll out the pastry to fit the top with a 2 cm overhang. Dampen the rim of the dish with water. Lay the pastry over the top, press the edges to seal, and trim the excess. Crimp the edges with a fork. Cut a small steam hole in the centre. Brush with beaten egg.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the pastry is deeply golden and the filling is bubbling through the steam vent. Rest for 5 minutes before serving.
